title: Why Lebrija tastes the way it does

lede.text: Lebrija's vines grow on flat farmland right beside the Guadalquivir marshes. The wines carry a subtle note that is sometimes described as salty.

chapters.title: Farmland at the edge of the marshes
paras: Lebrija lies in the Bajo Guadalquivir district, in the far southwest corner of the Iberian Peninsula on the right bank of the Guadalquivir. The district is framed by a triangle. One corner is the city of Sevilla. The other two are Doñana National Park and the Atlantic side of Cádiz province.

The vineyards sit in the campiña, the open farmland next to the marismas, the river marshes. That position shapes both the local climate and the soil. The protected zone covers just two municipalities in Sevilla province, Lebrija and El Cuervo.

Lebrija's wine tradition goes back beyond memory. The founding of Lebrija, as Lepriptza, is credited to the Phoenicians around the 7th century BC. In 1844 vines covered 324 aranzadas (145 ha) in 137 plots. In 1856 a larger area supplied 53 wine growers.

fly.label: Doñana National Park
fly.caption: One corner of the triangle that frames the Bajo Guadalquivir, with Sevilla and the Atlantic coast of Cádiz.

chapters.title: Long, hard summers in a climate softened by the Atlantic
paras: The climate is warm, of the continental Mediterranean type, softened by Atlantic currents. Autumn and spring are mild. Summer is long and harsh, with highs that can pass 40°. August is the hottest month.

Sunshine averages about 3,000 hours a year, about 65% of the maximum possible. Rain falls unevenly. October and December are the wettest months, along with March. Relative humidity averages about 70%. In July, while the grapes ripen, it drops to a low of between 49 and 56.

Frost is almost unknown and winters are short. Average temperatures always stay above 10°. Conditions for growth and for ripening are exceptional. They let the wines reach their character with relatively high yields. Night temperatures drop in summer, which gives outstanding conditions for wines of notable and characteristic aroma.

chapters.title: Albariza soil beside salty marsh
paras: Almost all the land is flat, with a slope under 3%. The few steeper plots lie in the foothills of the Sierra de Gibalbín, at 10 to 20%.
Albariza (whitish) soils, with good drainage and depth, dominate the vineyards and are considered excellent for vines. They stand out from the salty land of the neighbouring marshes.

fly.label: Sierra de Gibalbín
fly.caption: All of the zone's few steeper plots lie in these foothills, at slopes of 10 to 20%.

chapters.title: From dry flor wines to sweet Moscatel
paras: Lebrija makes white and red wines. It also makes vinos de licor (fortified wines), both dry and sweet. Palomino and Palomino Fino are the main white grapes. Moscatel de Alejandría and Sauvignon Blanc are also allowed. Six red grapes are allowed, among them Syrah and Tempranillo.
White wines are young and very pale, with a fruity aroma. They taste dry or off-dry. At least 60% of the grapes must come from the main white varieties.

Young reds have an intense fruity aroma and a vivid colour. Young oaked reds (tinto joven roble) are bright ruby, with an aroma of ripe fruit with hints of vanilla and coffee. Aged reds are deep cherry red and fleshy. They are full-bodied, with a velvety finish. Protected reds must age for at least 18 months, counted from 1 October of the harvest year.

Generosos are fortified wines (vinos de licor) made under a velo de flor, a veil of yeasts that grows by itself on the wine's surface. They use only Palomino or Palomino Fino grapes. Flor de Lebrija is straw yellow, sometimes with green glints. It has a pungent, delicate almond aroma and is light and dry, aged only under flor. Lebrija Old Vino Seco is amber to mahogany with a strong walnut aroma and plenty of body.

Lebrija Old Dulce is a generoso de licor, a fortified wine made from generoso. It has body and runs from amber to dark mahogany, with a pungent but muted aroma. Generosos and generosos de licor need an average age of at least three years before sale. They age in the classic criaderas y solera system of casks of different ages, or by vintage (añadas). They rest in oak casks (botas) of up to 600 litres. All protected wines must age in cellars in Lebrija or El Cuervo.

Dulce natural, natural sweet wine, is made with at least 85% Moscatel. The grapes are overripe and may be sun-dried or picked late. The must starts with at least 212 g/l of sugar. The wine can be called Moscatel. It is gold to mahogany, velvety and glyceric. Its aroma recalls honey, with caramel and raisins.
Mistela is made from filtered grape must, with wine alcohol added to stop fermentation partly or fully. It ends up between 15% and 18% alcohol.
Yields are capped at 15,000 kg per hectare for white grapes, and 10,000 kg for Sauvignon Blanc. For red grapes the cap is 11,250 kg, and 6,000 kg for Cabernet Sauvignon and Tintilla de Rota.

terms.text: A red or white wine aged at least 3 months in oak vessels.
A red or white wine aged at least 24 months in total, in oak barrels of up to 330 litres and in bottle, with at least 6 months in oak.
The same ageing in barrel and bottle for at least 36 months in total, with at least 12 months in oak.
The same ageing in barrel and bottle for at least 60 months in total, with at least 24 months in oak.
